content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler multiple vegetables, Stage 3 is a ready‑to‑serve puree blend of several vegetables designed for children from 12 months old. The blend contains carrot, broccoli, cauliflower, sweet potato and peas, steamed and finely pureed without added salt, sugar or preservatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend was developed by pediatricians and nutritionists to provide a varied diet during the transition from single‑vegetable purees to more complex meals.
All vegetables are grown without GMOs or synthetic pesticides.
The product undergoes gentle heat treatment that retains most B‑vitamins and carotenoids.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and ensures a long shelf life without preservatives.
The puree can be used as a base for first meals with meat or fish, making it easy to create balanced dishes.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Sweet potato and carrot provide provitamin A, which supports vision and immune function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Broccoli and cauliflower supply vitamin C, helping strengthen the immune system and improve iron absorption.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Peas and the vegetables overall promote healthy digestion and a balanced gut microbiome.

items.title: Supports brain development
items.content: Folate found in broccoli and peas is essential for the growth of neural cells in young children.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: No added salt makes the product safe for a child's developing kidneys.

items.title: Vegetable allergy
items.content: Some children may be allergic to one of the ingredients (e.g., peas). Introduce a small amount first and observe for reactions.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Although the puree is smooth, ensure the child does not try to swallow large lumps if the puree is thinned with liquid.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Broccoli and cauliflower contain low levels of oxalates; the current formula keeps them minimal.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The puree is ready to eat straight from the pack. It can be gently warmed to body temperature, mixed with breast milk, formula or water to adjust consistency, and used as a base for first meals with meat, fish or grains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened pack in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 7 days. Discard if the package is damaged or the smell changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Candy "Arachis Crunch" (peanut brittle) is a sweet caramel base studded with roasted peanut pieces and coated with a thin sugar glaze. The product has a crunchy texture, a sweet‑nutty flavor, and a bright golden color. It is made from sugar, glucose syrup, butter, roasted peanuts, vanilla and a pinch of salt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first peanut brittle-like confection appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
The traditional recipe requires rapid mixing of hot caramel with peanuts to achieve the characteristic brittle structure.
Peanuts are roasted to a golden hue, enhancing aroma and giving the candy its distinctive nutty taste.
Candy is often used as a decorative element for desserts, ice cream and cakes.
In many countries the product is sold under different brand names, but the core recipe remains unchanged.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Peanuts in the bar contain about 25 % protein, which helps support muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Peanuts provide monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that may support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals: magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: Peanuts supply magnesium and phosphorus, important for nerve function and bone health.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The candy rapidly replenishes energy due to its high simple sugar content.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are a strong allergen; individuals with a peanut allergy may experience severe reactions, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The large amount of sugar makes the product calorie‑dense and may contribute to tooth decay and blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of sugars and fats, the bar is energy‑dense; moderate portion sizes are recommended.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Industrial processing can generate small amounts of trans fats; choose products from reputable manufacturers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Candy "Arachis Crunch" can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, mixed into nut assortments, used in baking, sprinkled over ice cream, or incorporated into dessert platters. For young children, cut the bar into small pieces to reduce choking risk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life keep them refrigerated to prevent the caramel from cracking. Discard any bars that develop a burnt odor or change color.

content.title: About
content.content: Cod liver oil is a nutritional oil extracted from the livers of cod fish. It has long been taken as a supplement in Northern Europe and elsewhere and is a natural source of omega-3 fatty acids and the fat-soluble vitamins A and D. It is sold as a liquid and in capsules, sometimes flavored to reduce its fishy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cod liver oil has been used for centuries, traditionally to help prevent rickets in children.
Unlike most fish oils, which come from the flesh of fish, cod liver oil comes from the liver.
It provides EPA and DHA omega-3 fatty acids along with vitamin A and vitamin D.
Liquid cod liver oil has a strong fishy taste, so flavored versions and capsules are common.
Cod liver oil is a dietary supplement, so the amount of nutrients varies by product.

items.title: Source of omega-3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA support normal heart and brain function.

items.title: Provides vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and normal bone and muscle function.

items.title: Provides vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, skin, and immune function.

items.title: Traditional supplement
items.content: It is often used as a way to get vitamin D and omega-3 when the diet is low in fish and sun exposure is limited.

items.title: Available in different forms
items.content: It is sold as liquid, capsules, and flavored products.

items.title: Too much vitamin A
items.content: Cod liver oil is high in vitamin A. Excess vitamin A can be harmful, especially during pregnancy, so do not combine it with other vitamin A supplements and follow your doctor's advice.

items.title: Too much vitamin D
items.content: Excess vitamin D can raise calcium levels in the blood. Follow the label and your healthcare professional's advice.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: High doses of omega-3 and vitamin A or D may interact with medications such as blood thinners. People taking prescription drugs should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Side effects and allergies
items.content: Cod liver oil may cause fishy burps, heartburn, or nausea. It should be avoided by people allergic to fish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cod liver oil is taken as a liquid or in capsules, usually with a meal to reduce stomach upset. Follow the dose on the label or the advice of a healthcare professional, and ask a doctor or pharmacist before giving it to children. Flavored liquids or capsules can help with the taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cod liver oil in a tightly closed bottle in a cool, dark place, and refrigerate it after opening if the label says so. Keep it away from heat and light. Check the expiration date and discard oil that smells rancid.

corn-fresh-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-to-fat.title: Corn, fresh, cooked, fat added, NS (fat type)

content.title: About
content.content: Corn is a worldwide cultivated grain. This product consists of fresh ears that are boiled until tender and then sautéed with added fat. The preparation preserves the natural sweetness of the kernels and enhances their aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn was first domesticated over 7,000 years ago in Mexico and is one of the oldest cultivated crops.
There are more than 300 varieties of corn, differing in color, size, and flavor.
Beyond food, corn is used to produce bio‑fuel, plastics, and cosmetics.
The fat content of the final product depends on the type of added fat – vegetable or butter.
Carotenoids give some corn varieties their bright yellow hue.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn provides slowly digestible carbs that help maintain satiety over time.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and phenolic compounds help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in corn promotes healthy bowel movements.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Added vegetable fat enriches the dish with mono‑ and poly‑unsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to corn.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The added fat increases the energy density, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: While corn is naturally gluten‑free, processing may introduce trace gluten.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet corn can raise blood glucose levels, which is relevant for people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be enjoyed on its own, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a side dish. Garnish with fresh herbs or spices before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked corn in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-dark-gr.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with dark‑green vegetables, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs prepared as an omelet or scrambled, combined with dark‑green vegetables (such as spinach, broccoli or kale) and a small amount of added fat (butter, olive oil or other). Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while the vegetables are rich in vitamins, minerals and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark‑green vegetables contain chlorophyll, giving them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
Eggs are one of the few foods that contain all essential amino acids in adequate amounts.
A modest amount of fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from the vegetables.
The meal cooks quickly – usually 5‑7 minutes in a pan.
Variations exist worldwide: French "omelette aux épinards", Japanese "tamago to yasai no yaki", etc.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs supply complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain B12, riboflavin and biotin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Vitamins A, C, K and folate
items.content: Dark‑green vegetables provide vitamin A (vision), vitamin C (antioxidant), vitamin K (blood clotting) and folate (cell division).

items.title: Minerals – iron and calcium
items.content: Spinach and broccoli contribute iron and calcium, important for blood and bone health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Monounsaturated fats from the added oil and antioxidants in the vegetables help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach is high in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible persons.

items.title: Over‑heating fat
items.content: Cooking at too high a temperature can produce trans‑fats and harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and pepper. Heat 1‑2 tsp of oil in a skillet, add chopped dark‑green vegetables and sauté 2‑3 minutes. Pour the egg mixture over the vegetables and cook, stirring, until the desired consistency is reached (soft omelet or firmer scrambled eggs). Garnish with fresh herbs before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh eggs in the refrigerator for up to 4 weeks. Use vegetables within 2‑3 days, kept in an airtight container in the fridge. Cooked dish should be eaten within 2 hours at room temperature or refrigerated and consumed within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Gelato is an Italian frozen dessert known for its dense texture and lower overrun compared to traditional ice cream. The vanilla flavor is achieved with natural vanilla beans or extract, giving the product an aromatic, mildly sweet, and creamy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gelato is churned at a lower temperature than regular ice cream, preserving a more intense flavor.
Traditional gelato uses less cream and more milk, making it less fatty.
Vanilla flavor is often sourced from Madagascar beans, considered the best in the world.
In Italy gelato is served at about -12 °C, whereas ice cream is typically stored at -18 °C.
Gelato is frequently made without added stabilizers or emulsifiers, relying on the natural emulsification of eggs and sugar.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Compared with regular ice cream, gelato usually contains less cream, reducing the amount of saturated fat.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base provides calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs used in the recipe supply vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Vanilla antioxidants
items.content: Vanilla contains vanillin, an antioxidant that helps combat free radicals.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: The sugar in gelato is balanced with milk, leading to a smoother rise in blood glucose compared with pure sugary desserts.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Gelato contains dairy, so people with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Traditional gelato recipes include egg yolks, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite lower fat, gelato still contains a notable amount of sugar, which can be problematic for diabetics or those monitoring weight.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A typical serving (≈100 g) can contain 150–200 kcal, so portion control is important.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve gelato as scoops in cones, cups, or as a dessert portion. It pairs well with fresh fruit, nuts, chocolate sauce, or can be used as a base for milkshakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep gelato in the freezer at about -18 °C in an airtight container to prevent ice crystal formation. Before serving, let it sit 2–3 minutes at room temperature for a softer texture.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-and-poultr.title: Pasta with tomato-based sauce and poultry, ready‑to‑heat

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato sauce and chicken is a ready‑to‑heat meal that can be quickly warmed in a microwave or on the stove. The combination of tender chicken pieces, aromatic tomato sauce and al dente pasta provides a balanced flavor and a good amount of protein and carbohydrates for a complete lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tomato sauce is often made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, onion and spices, making it a rich source of lycopene.
Chicken is one of the most popular protein sources in ready meals because it cooks quickly and has a mild taste.
The pasta used is usually made from durum wheat, which gives a lower glycemic index compared with soft pasta.
The dish is commonly packaged in vacuum‑sealed or barrier films that preserve freshness and aroma until heating.
Microwave heating typically takes 3‑4 minutes, making it convenient for office lunches and travel.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that may support heart health and reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Durum wheat pasta releases energy slowly, helping to maintain satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and chicken contain vitamins B6 and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared correctly, the dish contains modest amounts of saturated fat, fitting a moderate diet.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready meals often contain added salt; people monitoring blood pressure should watch portion size.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to chicken and should avoid the product.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Food preservatives may be used to extend shelf life; sensitive individuals could experience reactions.

items.title: Thermal treatment
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave live bacteria; heat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in a microwave (800 W) for 3‑4 minutes, stirring halfway through, or on the stovetop while stirring until hot. Serve immediately, optionally garnish with fresh basil, grated Parmesan or a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in the refrigerator at 0 °C to +4 °C. Once opened, consume within 2‑3 days. Do not freeze, as the sauce texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Ground pork is minced pork meat obtained from various cuts of the carcass, most commonly from the shoulder, neck, and thigh. It has a soft texture, mild pork flavor, and a characteristic aroma. Ground pork is used in a wide range of dishes: patties, meatballs, sauces, fillings for pies and dumplings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ground pork is often added to sausages and hot dogs to improve juiciness and flavor.
Many traditional dishes around the world feature ground pork, such as Polish kibbeh, Italian ragù, and Russian kotleti.
Ground pork can be sold lean or with added fat, which influences taste and cooking properties.
When stored properly, fresh ground pork lasts up to 2 days in the fridge and up to 3 months in the freezer.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Ground pork provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and B12, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health, blood formation, and wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and a small amount of carbohydrate supplies sustained energy, useful for active individuals.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Ground pork can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella and E. coli. It must be cooked to an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Fat‑rich ground pork may contribute to elevated cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Added sodium in seasoned mixes
items.content: Pre‑seasoned ground pork can contain high salt levels, which is a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ground pork can be sautéed, braised, baked, or boiled. It is used for patties, meatballs, sauces, pie fillings, dumplings, and stuffed vegetables. If a leaner option is desired, excess fat can be drained after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh ground pork in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw completely in the fridge before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato fries are batata sticks that are deep‑fried or baked until crisp. They have a natural sweetness, golden color, and crunchy texture. Frequently served as a side or snack in fast‑food and restaurant menus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes contain more beta‑carotene than regular potatoes, giving the fries a bright orange hue.
They are often paired with a variety of sauces: garlic, chili, yogurt‑based, or honey‑mustard.
Compared to regular potatoes, sweet potatoes have a lower glycemic index, though they should still be eaten in moderation.
In some countries sweet potato fries are marketed as a healthier alternative to traditional fries.
Sweet potatoes are cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions but have adapted to temperate climates as well.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts antioxidant protection and immune function.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals in sweet potatoes combat free radicals, reducing the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant fat, so portion control is important.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature cooking can produce acrylamide, a potential toxin; lower temperatures or baking are safer.

items.title: Sweet potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to sweet potatoes; discontinue use if symptoms appear.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sweet potato fries hot, seasoned with salt, spices, or herbs. They can be enjoyed as a snack, in burgers, alongside salads, or as a side dish to meats. For a healthier option, bake the sticks with a light coating of oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fries in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or air‑fryer to restore crispness.

turkey-or-chicken-burger-on-white-bun.title: Turkey or Chicken Burger on White Bun

content.title: About
content.content: The turkey or chicken burger on a white bun is a hearty sandwich featuring lean poultry meat, fresh vegetables, and a soft white bun. It is popular in fast‑food and health‑focused restaurants thanks to its flavor and relatively low calorie count compared with beef burgers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey and chicken contain less saturated fat than beef, making them a healthier choice.
A white bun is typically made from wheat flour, water, yeast, and a small amount of sugar, giving it a soft texture.
The burger can be cooked on a grill or skillet while keeping the meat juicy.
Adding fresh vegetables (lettuce, tomato, onion) boosts the vitamin and mineral profile of the dish.
In some countries the burger is served with a yogurt or mustard sauce, adding probiotic benefits.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Turkey and chicken meat contain less saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A serving provides about 20‑25 g of protein, essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is high in niacin and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Meat supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, vital for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Added veggies increase dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to turkey or chicken.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor salmonella or campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: Sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Gluten in bun
items.content: White buns contain wheat, which may be problematic for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burger hot, split the bun, and layer the meat, lettuce, tomato slices, onion, and your chosen sauce. It can be eaten with hands, though a fork and knife work better if the bun is very soft.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled burger in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Separate components (meat, bun) can be frozen for up to 3 months; reheat thoroughly before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Greek nonfat yogurt is a thick, creamy dairy product made by double‑straining regular yogurt. Skim milk is used, and most of the whey is removed, resulting in a higher protein content and a velvety texture. Non‑fruit varieties are typically flavored with vanilla, honey, caramel, or spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt, known in Greece as “straggisto,” has been made for centuries.
Double‑straining can raise the protein content to about 10 g per 100 g, nearly double that of regular yogurt.
The nonfat version retains most of milk’s nutrients while containing virtually no fat.
Non‑fruit flavors often rely on natural flavor extracts and modest amounts of low‑calorie sweeteners such as stevia or erythritol.
Greek yogurt is frequently used as a substitute for sour cream or mayonnaise in recipes.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Protein supports muscle growth and repair and helps promote satiety.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: The near‑zero fat makes it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Skim milk provides a good amount of calcium for bone health, and many products are fortified with vitamin D.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Live cultures such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The combination of high protein and low sugar leads to a modest impact on blood glucose levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although some lactose is removed during straining, the product still contains enough to cause symptoms in lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to Greek yogurt.

items.title: Added sweeteners
items.content: Some brands use artificial sweeteners that can cause digestive upset in sensitive persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy Greek nonfat yogurt on its own, blend it into smoothies, use it as a base for dips, sauces, baked goods, or desserts. It pairs well with nuts, seeds, or a drizzle of honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the yogurt refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in its original container. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops off‑odors, mold, or an unusual texture.
